quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on Peirce's model: jamming, θ, D and crimp.

questions.q: A plain weave is 'jammed' in Peirce's sense when
options: the loom stops because of a warp break
the threads of both sets touch and the yarn has no straight portion between crossings
questions.explain: Jamming is the geometric limit: each yarn is a continuous arc around the crossing threads with no straight segment, so the cloth cannot be set any denser.

questions.q: In the formulas p = D sin θ and l = Dθ, D stands for
options: the sum of the warp and weft diameters, d₁ + d₂
questions.explain: D = d₁ + d₂ is the distance between the centres of the two yarns where they touch; for equal yarns D = 2d.

questions.q: Crimp as a fraction is defined as
questions.explain: Crimp is the yarn length per crossing divided by the spacing of the threads it crosses, minus 1: 2.094 ÷ 1.732 − 1 = 0.209 for equal yarns.

questions.q: In a jammed plain weave the two crimp heights add up to D: h₁ + h₂ = D.
questions.explain: Each yarn's crimp height equals the other yarn's diameter when jammed, so h₁ + h₂ = d₂ + d₁ = D.

questions.q: The angle θ in Peirce's model is
options: the twill angle on the cloth face
the angle at which the yarn leaves the crossing thread
the shed angle on the loom
questions.explain: θ measures how steeply the yarn climbs off the thread it wraps; everything else in the jammed geometry follows from it.

questions.q: For equal yarns in a jammed plain weave, θ equals
questions.explain: With h = d and D = 2d, 1 − cos θ = 0.5, so cos θ = 0.5 and θ = 60°.

questions.q: Rib fabrics consume far more warp yarn than their weight suggests because
options: the warp crimp is about 57 % while the weft is nearly straight
rib weaves have more ends per inch than cloth can hold
questions.explain: The fine warp wraps half-way round the thick weft pair, giving l₁ = 4.71 d₁ over 3 d₁ of cloth; the thick weft lies straight.

questions.q: Real plain cloths look fully covered at K around 1000–1400 rather than at the theoretical 1542, because real yarns are flattened.
questions.explain: A flattened yarn covers more width than a circle of the same area, so full cover is reached below the circular-yarn limit.

questions.q: The 'modular length' of the 2/2 twill in the lecture is
options: half of the four-thread repeat, spanning 2p
the full repeat of four threads
questions.explain: Each thread interlaces after every second crossing thread, so half the repeat (one arc plus one straight float) is the unit: 2p = 2.732 d.

questions.q: In the crimp calculator the warp spacing p₁ is computed from θ₂, the weft angle, because
options: warp and weft angles are always equal
the spacing between warp ends is set by how the weft bends round them
questions.explain: The gap between two warp ends is the chord of the weft's arc around them, D sin θ₂; likewise the weft spacing follows the warp's angle θ₁.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The Peirce relationships and how crimp and cover respond to the yarn diameters.

questions.q: Thread spacing in the jammed structure is
questions.explain: p is the chord across the arc: D sin θ. Dθ is the arc length l and D(1 − cos θ) the height h.

questions.q: The yarn length per crossing l = Dθ requires θ in
questions.explain: Arc length = radius × angle only in radians: 60° = π/3 = 1.047 rad gives l = 2 × 1.047 = 2.094 d.

questions.q: Crimp height is
questions.explain: The yarn centre rises from the crossing thread's centre by D(1 − cos θ); for equal yarns that is 2d × 0.5 = d.

questions.q: Equal yarns, θ = 60°, D = 2d. Thread spacing p in units of d (sin 60° = 0.8660), to three decimals?
questions.explain: p = D sin θ = 2 × 0.866 = 1.732 d, that is √3 d.

questions.q: Equal yarns, θ = 60° = π/3 radians, D = 2d. Yarn length per crossing l in units of d, to three decimals?
When the weft is much thicker than the warp in a jammed plain weave,
options: the thick weft takes most of the crimp
the fine warp takes most of the crimp
questions.explain: The fine yarn has to climb over the thick one: with d₂ = 2d₁ the warp crimp is about 31 % and the weft only about 13 %.

questions.q: The cover factor in the crimp calculator is
questions.explain: K = 2670 × d/p is the tex cover factor scaled so that touching threads (d = p) give 2670; 28 belongs to the Ne system.

questions.q: With equal yarns a 2/2 twill has less crimp than a plain weave.
questions.explain: The straight float adds length without adding interlacing: 13.1 % crimp in the 2/2 twill against 20.9 % in plain.

questions.q: If θ increases (the yarn climbs more steeply), the crimp
questions.explain: Crimp = θ ÷ sin θ − 1 for a jammed yarn, and θ ÷ sin θ grows with θ: 60° gives 20.9 %, 70.5° gives about 31 %.

questions.q: Making the weft twice as thick as the warp (d₂ = 2d₁) changes the warp spacing p₁ (in units of d₁) from 1.732 to
questions.explain: p₁ = D sin θ₂ with D = 3 and cos θ₂ = 2/3, so p₁ = 3 × 0.745 = 2.236; 2.828 is the weft spacing p₂.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work the jammed-plain geometry for equal and unequal yarns and the 2/2 twill.

questions.q: Equal yarns: l = 2.094 d and p = 1.732 d. Crimp as a percentage, to one decimal?
Equal yarns with p = 1.732 d. Cover factor K = 2670 × d ÷ p, to the nearest whole number?
questions.explain: 2670 ÷ 1.732 = 1,542 — the densest plain square cloth possible with circular yarns.

questions.q: Weft twice the warp: d₁ = 1, d₂ = 2, D = 3. The warp angle has cos θ₁ = 1/3, so sin θ₁ = 0.9428. Weft spacing p₂ = D sin θ₁, to three decimals?
Same yarns (D = 3). The weft angle has cos θ₂ = 2/3, so sin θ₂ = 0.7454. Warp spacing p₁ = D sin θ₂, to three decimals?
D = 3 d₁ and the warp angle θ₁ = 70.53° = 1.231 radians. Warp length per crossing l₁ = Dθ₁, to two decimals?
Warp length per crossing l₁ = 3.693 d₁ and the weft spacing it crosses is p₂ = 2.828 d₁. Warp crimp as a percentage, to one decimal?
questions.explain: 3.693 ÷ 2.828 = 1.306; the warp crimp is about 30.6 % (the lecture's 29.5 % uses rounded angles).

questions.q: With d₁ = 1 and p₁ = 2.236, the warp cover factor K₁ = 2670 × d₁ ÷ p₁, to the nearest whole number?
questions.explain: 2670 ÷ 2.236 = 1,194 — the fine warp is spread out by the thick weft.

questions.q: With d₂ = 2 and p₂ = 2.828, the weft cover factor K₂ = 2670 × d₂ ÷ p₂, to the nearest whole number?
2/2 twill, equal yarns: modular length 2p = 2.732 d spans two threads. K = 2670 × 2 ÷ 2.732 is
questions.explain: 2670 × 2 ÷ 2.732 = 1,955; 977 forgets that the modular length covers two threads.

questions.q: 2/2 twill, equal yarns: yarn length per modular length l = 3.09 d over 2.732 d. The crimp is
questions.explain: 3.09 ÷ 2.732 = 1.131, so 13.1 % — lower than plain weave's 20.9 %.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Using crimp in the costing office and the design room.

questions.q: Costing a warp-rib fabric with a fine warp and a thick weft, the yarn allowance should assume
options: about 57 % extra warp length and almost no extra weft
about 57 % extra weft and no extra warp
equal crimp of about 21 % in both
questions.explain: In the warp rib the warp wraps half-way round the double weft (l₁ = 4.71 d₁ over 3 d₁) while the weft lies straight.

questions.q: A test shows 100 cm of plain cloth yields 121 cm of straightened warp yarn. This cloth is
options: close to the jammed limit for equal yarns (20.9 %)
questions.explain: 21 % crimp is essentially the jammed equal-yarn value, so the warp can hardly be packed closer.

questions.q: A 50 cm length of cloth gives 58 cm of straightened yarn. Crimp as a percentage?
questions.explain: 58 ÷ 50 = 1.16, so the crimp is 16 %.

questions.q: A plain square cloth of circular yarns is already at K = 1,542. The designer wants it denser. The option is
options: change to a 2/2 twill, which can be jammed at K = 1,955
questions.explain: 1,542 is the jammed limit for plain weave; a twill interlaces less often and can be set to 1,955. More ends simply will not fit.

questions.q: A plain cloth at K = 1,300 can look fully covered even though the circular model needs 1,542.
questions.explain: Real yarns flatten and spread, so full visual cover is reached at about 1000–1400 in practice.

questions.q: For a 2/2 twill with equal yarns, the warp yarn length to buy per 100 m of cloth, allowing only for crimp, is about
questions.explain: Twill crimp is 13.1 %, so 113 m; 121 m is the plain-weave figure and 157 m the warp rib.

questions.q: A warp-rib fabric has 57 % warp crimp. How many metres of warp yarn are needed per 100 m of cloth, ignoring wastage?
questions.explain: 100 × 1.57 = 157 m of warp per 100 m of cloth.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill with 13.1 % crimp: metres of warp yarn per 100 m of cloth, to one decimal?
A merchandiser specifies a fine warp with a weft twice as thick in plain weave. Which yarn needs the larger crimp allowance?
options: Neither — crimp is zero in jammed cloth
questions.explain: The fine warp climbs over the thick weft: warp crimp ≈ 31 %, weft ≈ 13 % (lecture rounding 29.5 % / 12.2 %).

questions.q: In the lecture's warp rib (d₂ = 2d₁) the weft lies straight with essentially no crimp.
questions.explain: The thick wefts lie side by side in pairs at 1.5 d₂ spacing and the warp does all the bending round them.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder review: twill and rib geometry, common slips and two-step reasoning.

questions.q: 2/2 twill, equal yarns: the modular length is one jammed spacing (1.732 d) plus a straight float of d. Its value in units of d, to three decimals?
questions.explain: 1.732 + 1 = 2.732 d — half of the four-thread repeat.

questions.q: 2/2 twill, equal yarns: yarn length over the modular length is one jammed arc (2.094 d) plus a straight d. Total in units of d, to three decimals?
Warp rib: the warp wraps a half circle of diameter 3 d₁. Warp length per repeat l₁ = π × 3 ÷ 2, in units of d₁, to two decimals?
questions.explain: Half the circumference of a circle of diameter 3 d₁: π × 3 ÷ 2 = 4.71 d₁.

questions.q: Warp rib: l₁ = 4.71 d₁ over 3 d₁ of cloth. Warp crimp as a percentage, to one decimal?
A student calculates the crimp of the equal-yarn plain weave as h ÷ p = 1 ÷ 1.732 = 57.7 %. The mistake is
options: using the crimp height instead of the yarn length: crimp is l ÷ p − 1
questions.explain: Crimp compares the yarn length with the cloth length it occupies, 2.094 ÷ 1.732 − 1 = 20.9 %; the height h is a different quantity.

questions.q: In a jammed plain weave with d₁ = 1 and d₂ = 2, the warp crimp height h₁ is
questions.explain: When jammed each yarn's crimp height equals the other yarn's diameter, so h₁ = d₂ = 2 and h₂ = d₁ = 1, summing to D = 3.

questions.q: Why does the warp angle satisfy cos θ₁ = 1/3 when d₂ = 2d₁?
options: Because h₁ = D(1 − cos θ₁) must equal d₂ = 2 with D = 3
questions.explain: 3(1 − cos θ₁) = 2 gives cos θ₁ = 1/3, so θ₁ = 70.5°; the weft, with h₂ = 1, has cos θ₂ = 2/3 and θ₂ = 48.2°.

questions.q: In the jammed equal-yarn plain weave the yarn is about one-fifth longer than the cloth it lies in.
questions.explain: Crimp is 20.9 %, so 100 cm of cloth contains about 121 cm of yarn.

questions.q: With equal yarns, which structure has the lowest crimp in the lecture?
questions.explain: The twill's straight float adds cloth length without extra bending; the warp rib is the extreme in the other direction.

questions.q: With d₂ = 2 and p₂ = 2.828, the weft's relative cover is K₂ ÷ 2670 = d₂ ÷ p₂. Give three decimals.
questions.explain: 2 ÷ 2.828 = 0.707 — the thick wefts cover about 71 % of the cloth length, matching K₂ = 1,888.
